newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian insurers optimistic on growth.
newsitem.headline: Estonian insurers optimistic on growth.

text.p: The tiny Baltic state of Estonia is seen as having the most advanced banking market in the region and analysts said on Friday that its insurance sector was also set for good growth.
Estonian banks have already attracted lots of Western investment since the country quit the former Soviet Union in 1991 and instituted market reforms.
With a bit of help from lawmakers, analysts said that insurance companies may also experience the same kind of growth as banks, most of which now have insurance arms.

They also said that as Estonians have got used to using bank cards and other more sophisticated bank services, people who until recently never thought of needing insurance would more and more be insuring themselves and their goods.
The biggest potential for growth is seen in the life insurance market although non-life has so far dominated.
"There could be a boom if some tax allowances are made," said Mart Einpalu, chairman of Hansapank Insurance, part of Estonia's largest bank, Hansapank.
"The increase depends on the insurance companies mostly, on their abilities to catch customers and sell a good image," Einpalu told Reuters.

Finnish firms have also become interested in the market of their Estonian neighbour, just 80 kms across the Gulf of Finland, and Pohjola recently bought a stake in life insurer Seesam-Elu with Estonian bank Uhispank.

Insurance companies say one of the impeding factors to the growth of the life market is that pension reform has not yet been implemented and that income tax is charged on life insurance payments, which companies hope to be changed.
The life insurance market in Estonia, which has a population of just 1.5 million, was worth 65 million kroons in 1996 and is estimated to grow to 100 million kroons this year.
Insurance companies collected 840 million kroons in premiums last year, which is up from 1995 by 52 percent. Most premiums came from traffic insurance: 335 million kroons.

Eduard Saul, sales group director of largest insurance firm Eesti Kindlustus (Estonian Insurance), part of second-largest bank Hoiupank, said the life market was too small at the moment as it was just under 10 percent of the total market.
"An explosive increase may be possible after some political decisions are taken," he said.
He said total insurance premiums collected were estimated to reach one billion kroons at the end of this year and that his company expected to have a quarter of the market.
Heido Vitsur, an advisor to the prime minister on economic affairs, said that further growth in the life-insurance market depended on people's earnings and slowing inflation.
"As earnings are on the increase and inflation on the decrease, life insurance may become interesting," Vitsur said.
Further growth in the compulsory traffic insurance, which has the biggest or almost 40 percent of the total market, depends on new car sales, Vitsur said.
